newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Europe presses Britain to honour mad cow cull.
newsitem.headline: Europe presses Britain to honour mad cow cull.

text.p: EU states pressed Britain on Monday to honour a plan to eradicate mad cow disease and avert what the Agriculture Commissioner said was the biggest crisis in the 40-year-old European Union.

"The beef crisis is the biggest crisis we ever had in the European Union," Commissioner Franz Fischler told reporters as EU Agriculture ministers sought to persuade Britain to stick to a four-month-old pact to eradicate the disease.

Britain's Agriculture Minister, Douglas Hogg, appeared to be backing away from the kind of conflict with his EU partners which led to London blocking dozens of EU decisions in protest at a ban on its beef exports because of mad cow disease.

He said Britain would work with its EU partners to implement an agreement thrashed out at an EU summit in Florence under which Britain was supposed to slaughter large numbers of cattle to get a world ban on its beef exports lifted.

But Hogg made no reference to his government's decision last week to suspend the cull of an additional 147,000 young cattle because, it said, new evidence showed it would not speed up the elimination of Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE).
The announcement infuriated Britain's EU partners who are already weary of Britain's go-it-alone attitude on EU policies ranging from a single currency to common security.
"We are going to work together within the Florence agreement," Hogg told reporters when EU Ministers visited an Irish farm during informal three-day talks in this southern Irish town.

But he did not appear to have pacified several of his colleagues angered at what they see as a politically-motivated and unilateral decision to go back on a pact painstakingly worked out at the summit to end Britain's policy of blocking EU decision-making.
Fischler said: "If the British do not implement the cull, then it is clearly a breach of the Florence agreement.
"Every step taken in the wrong direction does not help to restore consumer confidence," he added.
Many EU states fear the British decision will only worsen a community-wide fall in beef consumption because of fears over BSE and cut away at farmers' incomes.
Britain says research by Oxford academics shows that killing younger cattle will not speed up the elimination of BSE which will die out naturally, they believe, early next century.
It has submitted the research to the EU Commission and scientists for study, but no decision is expected from either body until the end of next month.
Britain's European partners appear to be losing patience with what they see as a British problem which has now spread to the European continent.
"We don't have BSE in Austria but we do have all the problems on the (beef) market," said Wilhelm Molterer, the Austrian Agriculture Minister.
Denmark's Minister, Henrik Dam Kristensen,told Reuters: "This agreement (Florence) will have to stand.
"It could only be changed on a recommendation of EU scientists but for now there is no reason for change," he said.
Fischler said there would be formal discussion of Britain's attitude at talks on Tuesday when all the ministers sit round the conference table for the first time during their visit.
He said farmers and consumers needed a clear message from Britain that it would go ahead with the Florence plan.
"We need clear proposals and clear signals to the farmers and to the consumers and that must be the discussion tomorrow," he said.
